candidates.title: Identity
candidates.reason: A storm strands ten apparent strangers at a motel, where sequential murders, numbered room keys, disappearing bodies and conflicting suspicions make the culprit hunt a sustained puzzle. A parallel last-minute hearing for Malcolm Rivers becomes an explanatory thread, and the motel events' relationship to that hearing eventually reframes the entire scenario; a final killer-identity reversal follows. The film therefore has recurring clues and suspect changes, but the most consequential reframing is concentrated in its later portion, so high twist impact must not be confused with near-constant progressive revelation. Ebert describes the motel murders and hearing as intercut strands; the complete IMDb synopsis resolves both, while Slant identifies an initially taut whodunit but argues that the final psychological explanation is implausible and unsatisfying. Dark, controlled motel staging and brisk crosscutting support suspense, while limited physical action and disputed final logic are material weaknesses.

candidates.title: Headhunters
candidates.reason: Roger Brown's planned Rubens theft turns into an escalating pursuit by Clas Greve. New discoveries are distributed across the film: the suspected affair, Ove's poisoning, Greve's apparent ability to track Roger, a GPS-gel explanation, Lotte's concealed allegiance and the corporate-espionage motive. Roger's countermeasures culminate in deliberately manipulated security footage and a staged police narrative. The complete IMDb synopsis supports repeated causal revelations and tactical reversals rather than a single finale-only twist; Ebert emphasizes its labyrinth of double-crosses and sustained chase, while Critic's Notebook praises pace, violence and midflight reassessment of characters. Its first stretch emphasizes heist setup and marital insecurity more than investigation, and its later explanations are tidier than some critics accept. The Guardian criticizes the gore and tonal disjunction. Military background describes Greve, but the story is not a military-operations thriller.
